title: Empty, and never used up
hook: the Tao is empty like a bowl yet never runs dry; it blunts sharp edges and unties knots (Tao Te Ching 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter three, and your line was no contest. Which race did you drop out of? Chapter three emptied minds of wanting. Chapter four says the Tao itself is empty. Day one thousand sixty-six.

A necklace chain comes out of the drawer in one tight knot. The first move is to pull: grab two ends and tug. And the knot gets smaller and harder, and now it's a little bead of metal you could never pick apart. The way out is the opposite of pulling. Lay it flat on the table. Loosen the middle with the tip of a pin. Give the loops room. Slowly, the knot opens, not because anyone forced it, but because someone made space inside it. Chapter four of the Tao Te Ching is about that kind of space.
screen: `A CHAIN IN ONE TIGHT KNOT.` → `PULLING MAKES IT WORSE.` → `MAKE ROOM INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: First, empty like a bowl. The chapter opens by comparing the Tao to the emptiness of a vessel. You can use it and use it, and it never fills up and never runs dry. That's strange arithmetic. Full things run out. A bowl that's already full can't take anything else. It's the empty part of the bowl that does the work. Second, deep, and nobody's child. The chapter calls the Tao deep, so deep it seems like the ancestor of everything. Then it ends with a shrug that's almost funny: it says it doesn't know whose child the Tao is. It seems to come before even the Lord on High. The book doesn't claim to know where the Tao came from. It only says the Tao seems to come before even that. Third, blunt the sharp, untie the knot. In the middle of the chapter comes the line that gives today its practice. In Legge's words: "We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things." Sharp points: the cutting remark, the edge in a voice. Complications: tangles of the kind the chain was in. The same lines come back later in the book, in chapter fifty-six, as if the old master wanted them heard twice. Fourth, soften the glare. The chapter goes on: soften your brightness, and settle in with the dust of everyone else. Not shining at people. Not standing above the tangle. Getting down next to it, the way you'd lay a chain flat on the table and give it room.
screen: `EMPTY LIKE A BOWL.` · `DEEP, AND NOBODY'S CHILD.` · `BLUNT THE SHARP, UNTIE THE KNOT.` · `SOFTEN THE GLARE.` · then, large: `UNTIE THE KNOT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to untie one knot. Settle, and breathe. Find one tangle in your life right now: a misunderstanding with someone, a messy email thread, a drawer, a decision you've been tugging at for weeks. Don't try to solve it in the next two minutes. Just stop pulling on it. Breathe into the middle of it and give it some room, the way you'd loosen a chain with the tip of a pin. Ask what one small loop could be loosened first. If you pray, you can bring the knot into prayer. If you don't, just keep breathing space into it. The bell holds the time.
Empty. In chapter four, the Tao is empty like a bowl, used and used and never used up, and the chapter says it doesn't know whose child it is. Today's word.
Your line: untie the knot. Today, take that one small loop you found and loosen it: one honest message, one drawer, one first step. Day one thousand sixty-six.

howItsDone: Some Taoist meditation teachers use chapter four's lines about blunting sharp points and untying tangles as a reminder to soften and settle before sitting.

original.note: Chinese, chōng: empty, hollow. The word chapter four uses for the Tao's emptiness.

trapdoor: what you thought: empty means nothing there, nothing useful.
what it means: in chapter four the Tao is empty like a bowl, and the emptiness is what's used; it never fills up and never runs dry.
what a scholar hears: the chapter's four lines on blunting, untying, softening and settling with the dust return in chapter fifty-six.

notes: Legge quotation from chapter 4 verify wording.

Paraphrased: 'the Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel'; 'as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things'; 'I do not know whose son it is. It might appear to have been before God.' The script renders Legge's 'God' (帝, di) as 'the Lord on High'; a Keeper may prefer another rendering.
The claim that the four lines recur in chapter 56 is from the Chinese text; confirm.
沖 chōng: some editions read 盅 (an empty vessel); the note keeps to the common received text.
Day 1060 previewed the empty bowl from chapter 11; this day keeps chapter 4's vessel brief and leans on the knot instead, so chapter 11 (day 1073) still has its own image.
Editor pass: 'the Tao was there first' softened to match the text ('might appear to have been before'); the word line now says the chapter doesn't know whose child it is, not 'nobody knows'.
